nodes.7: Language-based security uses type systems and static checks to prevent vulnerabilities, ensuring safe code via compiler-enforced guarantees.

nodes.12: Screened subnet uses three subnets (external, DMZ, internal) with routers to isolate networks, enhancing security by requiring intruders to traverse multiple barriers.
nodes.13: Machine code consists of CPU-executable instructions, translated from higher-level languages via assemblers, using opcodes for arithmetic/logic operations.
nodes.14: James G. Mitchell developed compilers (FORTRAN, Euclid) and worked on Mesa/C++ at Xerox/Sun, contributing to programming languages and hardware design.
nodes.15: Computer viruses replicate via code insertion, spread via files/networks, and evade detection; antivirus software uses signatures/heuristics to counter threats like ransomware and polymorphic malware.

nodes.17: Multilevel security (MLS) protects info across classifications using mandatory access controls like Bell-LaPadula, with trusted systems like SELinux and Solaris Trusted Extensions.
nodes.18: Intermediate representations (IR) enable compilers to optimize code via abstract forms like three-address code, aiding cross-language/target portability (e.g., LLVM IR).
nodes.19: Tim Teitelbaum pioneered integrated development environments (IDEs) and incremental computation, co-founded Grammatech, and advanced program analysis tools.
nodes.20: computer scientist known for APL\360 compiler (Hopper Award 1973), co-founded I.P. Sharp Associates, contributed to Subalgol/Algol 60 compilers, and IPSANET development.
nodes.21: computer scientist renowned for Lisp's Gabriel Benchmarks, "Worse is Better" essay, roles at Lucid Inc., open-source advocacy, and poetry; ACM Fellow 2004.

nodes.0: Proposes EMMA, a differential learning rule using kernel density estimation to optimize entropy, applied to 3D model alignment and MRI corruption correction.
nodes.1: Explores overcomplete representations for feature extraction, emphasizing sparse coding and efficient signal decomposition.
nodes.2: Uses temporal association in recurrent networks with Hebbian learning to develop viewpoint-invariant face recognition via temporal proximity of views.

nodes.4: Enhances blind audio source separation using overdetermined mixtures and MBLMS, improving performance with additional sensors.
nodes.5: Extracts coherent depth from stereograms via competitive anti-Hebbian learning in unsupervised neural networks.

nodes.9: Combines ICA and attractor networks for viewpoint-invariant face recognition, outperforming PCA in pose variance.
nodes.10: Learns efficient overcomplete image codes (Gabor-like) via sparse coding, excelling in denoising and pixel recovery.
nodes.11: Proposes recurrent NNs with adaptive learning rates for faster blind separation, enabling chaotic output switching in non-stationary signals.
nodes.12: Uses multi-layer networks with local learning rules for blind image separation, enabling VLSI implementation and sequential source extraction.
nodes.13: Addresses real-room speaker separation using frequency-domain infomax to handle non-minimum phase filters.
nodes.14: Employs predictability minimization to learn edge and feature detectors from raw images without preprocessing.
nodes.15: Develops factorial codes via predictability minimization, yielding distributed non-redundant representations for segmentation and novelty detection.
nodes.16: Introduces fast fixed-point ICA algorithm with cubic convergence, requiring no user parameters for blind source separation.

nodes.5: TCP-based DoS attack overwhelming servers with SYN requests; countered via RFC 4987 methods like connection limits.
nodes.6: Denial-of-service attacks overwhelm systems via floods, disrupting access; includes DDoS, application-layer attacks, and historical large-scale incidents.
nodes.7: Zombie computers compromised in botnets for spam/DDoS, often unbeknownst to owners, used in coordinated attacks like Spews and mobile botnets.
nodes.8: Seamoby protocol aids mobile router discovery, enabling fast handovers via neighbor lists, aligned with 3GPP SON standards for wireless networks.
nodes.9: Hashcash proof-of-work system thwarts spam/cryptocurrency mining using SHA-1 hashes; requires computational effort to validate transactions/emails.
nodes.10: SQL Slammer 2003 worm exploited unpatched SQL Server via UDP, crashing routers globally, spreading rapidly via buffer overflow.
nodes.11: Code Red 2001 worm targeted IIS servers, caused DDoS against White House, used buffer overflow, and had variants infecting hundreds of thousands.
nodes.12: GEORGE OS series developed by ICT in the 1960s, featuring batch processing, multitasking, and evolving through versions 1-4, later obsolete but preserved in emulation.
nodes.13: Client computing categorizes systems as thick, thin, or hybrid, defining how clients interact with servers in distributed networks.
nodes.14: Galeon was a GNOME-focused Gecko browser, popular in the 2000s until a dev split led to Epiphany; discontinued in 2008.
nodes.15: Internet Protocol (IP) routes datagrams via addresses, with IPv4/IPv6 versions, enabling internetworking through packet headers and addressing.
nodes.16: Aanval is a SIEM tool using Snort/Suricata, offering web-based security monitoring since 2003, featured in O'Reilly publications.
nodes.17: BGP hijacking involves illegitimate route takeovers,如2008's YouTube Pakistan incident, mitigated via RPKI and filtering.
nodes.18: Nimda worm (2001) exploited multiple vectors, affecting Windows systems post-9/11, notable for rapid spread and multi-vector attacks.
nodes.19: GNUstep replicates Objective-C frameworks for cross-platform development, compatible with Cocoa/OpenStep, part of the GNU project.
nodes.20: Data center security combines physical safeguards and virtual tools (firewalls, IDS) to prevent breaches, DDoS, and insider threats.
nodes.21: LOIC is an open-source DDoS tool used by Anonymous, enabling coordinated attacks but posing legal risks under CFAA.

nodes.23: RocksDB is a high-performance key-value database (forked from LevelDB), optimized for SSDs, used in Facebook, CockroachDB, and MongoDB.
nodes.24: NTP server misuse includes DDoS via Monlist requests, router firmware flaws causing traffic floods, and solutions like KOD packets and RFC updates to mitigate issues.
